record.paper_title: Some open questions on morphological operators and representations in the deep learning era: A personal vision
record.original_question: For ultrametric convolutional neural networks operating on dendrogram or rooted-tree representations of data, how can the convolution operation be learned efficiently, how should max-pooling and unpooling layers be defined, and are there additional layers specifically useful for this type of neural network?

evidence.quote: How to efficiently learn the convolution operation on ultrametric convolutional neural networks? How to define the max-pooling and unpooling-layers on ultrametric convolutional neural networks? Are there specific layers useful in this kind of neural networks?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
An ultrametric space is a metric space (X, d) in which the distance d satisfies the strong triangle inequality d(x, z) ≤ max{d(x, y), d(y, z)} for all x, y, z ∈ X. Finite ultrametric spaces are in bijection with rooted trees (dendrograms) whose leaves are the points of X, where the distance between two leaves equals the height of their lowest common ancestor.

Consider data represented as points in a finite ultrametric space, equivalently as leaves of a rooted tree (dendrogram) endowed with a height function on internal nodes. A convolutional neural network operating on such data is called an ultrametric convolutional neural network: each layer takes as input a function f : X → ℝ^c on the leaves (or more generally on the nodes) of an ultrametric/dendrogram structure and outputs another such function, in a way compatible with the hierarchical/ultrametric geometry.

Address the following:

(a) Define a notion of convolution operator on functions over a finite ultrametric space (or its associated dendrogram) which (i) respects the ultrametric/hierarchical structure, (ii) has a finite parameterization that can be learned by gradient-based optimization, and (iii) admits an efficient algorithm (specify its computational complexity in terms of the number of leaves and the depth of the tree).

(b) Define max-pooling and unpooling layers for such networks, in a way consistent with the ultrametric structure: max-pooling should aggregate values along subtrees (e.g., children of an internal node) to produce a function on a coarsened dendrogram, and unpooling should provide a corresponding inverse-like operation suitable for encoder–decoder architectures. State precise definitions and prove that the resulting operators are equivariant or invariant under the appropriate isomorphisms of dendrograms.

(c) Identify additional layer types that are specifically meaningful for ultrametric convolutional neural networks (for example, layers exploiting the lattice of internal nodes, the partial order of subtrees, or non-Archimedean arithmetic) and motivate their usefulness either theoretically or by an explicit construction.
artifact.status_search_result: A web search did not surface any work that gives a comprehensive answer to defining efficient convolution, max-pooling/unpooling, and additional dedicated layers for ultrametric (dendrogram-based) convolutional neural networks. Related work touches on pooling variants and ultrametric contour features but does not resolve the design questions posed. The problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Pooling Methods in Deep Neural Networks, a Review
status_evidence.snippet: Survey of pooling methods in deep networks; does not address ultrametric/dendrogram-based convolutional layers.
status_evidence.claim: No standard formulation of convolution and pooling on ultrametric/dendrogram domains is reported.

status_evidence.title: A New Pooling Approach Based on Zeckendorf's Theorem for Texture Transfer Information
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses pooling configurations that emphasize ultrametric contours, but not learnable convolution on ultrametric/dendrogram inputs.
status_evidence.claim: Existing literature touches on ultrametric features in pooling but does not resolve the design of ultrametric CNN layers.
